e.t: This Greek word means “lead” or “pass.” It describes directing or bringing someone or something along, and it can also express passing through or proceeding from one place or point to another. As a verb, its exact sense depends on what is being led or passed and the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 223 times, showing that it is a regularly used word for movement or guidance.

“Lord” refers to a person recognized as a master, ruler, or one worthy of respect. It is a noun used as a title or designation rather than an action or description. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs once, at Jeremiah 41:5. The available lexical meaning is simply “Lord,” so its more specific force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being addressed or described.

Athin is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it functions as an individual’s name. Athin appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 8:25. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s specific role in that genealogy cannot be explained further. Its basic meaning is simply the personal name “Athin.”

Aithiel, also rendered Ethil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 11:7. The available information identifies the name and its use as a proper name, but does not provide a further definition or explain the person’s role. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Aitam, also rendered Etam, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in three verses, all within Chronicles. The available lexical definition identifies it only as the name Aitam or Etam; without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified here. Its meaning is therefore best understood as a personal or place name preserved in the biblical record, with the immediate context determining whom or what it names.

This adjective describes something “untameable”—not able to be brought under control or restrained. It presents its subject as resistant to being subdued, rather than simply difficult or inconvenient. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in 3 Maccabees. Without the verse text, its precise force in either passage cannot be narrowed further; its stable lexical sense is the quality of being untameable.

This verb means “spring” or “leap,” describing a sudden upward or forward movement. It can express the act of jumping rather than merely moving from one place to another. The word appears 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages from Judges, 1 Samuel, Job, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains energetic movement by springing or leaping.

Amaltheia is a proper name, referring to a specific woman named Amaltheia, also rendered Amalthia. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Job 42:14. Because it is a personal name rather than a common noun or descriptive term, its meaning is chiefly its identification of that individual. The surrounding verse text is not included here, so the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further.

Ammanith is a proper name, preserved as “Ammanith” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:52. Because the available wording gives only the name itself and no surrounding verse text, its precise identity and role must be determined from that passage. The word therefore functions as a specific name, not as a general term describing an object, action, quality, or relationship.

This Greek LXX verb means “push back” or “stop short.” It describes drawing back instead of continuing forward, whether by resisting movement or suddenly holding back. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages from Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Ezekiel. Its basic sense remains focused on a physical or purposeful retreat, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being resisted or interrupted.

The word refers to a political opponent—someone who stands against another in a political or civic setting. As a verb, it expresses opposing or acting as an opponent in public affairs, rather than merely describing private disagreement. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 4:1. The surrounding wording would be needed to explain the particular situation more fully, but its central sense is opposition in political terms.

This Greek LXX verb means “absent”: it describes someone or something being away or not present. It is a straightforward word for absence rather than a term that, by itself, explains why someone is away or what that absence means in a particular situation. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, including Exodus, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether the word simply states absence or contributes to a larger movement or event.

This Greek LXX verb means “take down a tent.” It describes the action of dismantling or removing a tent after it has served as a dwelling or temporary shelter. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 13:18. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense is the physical act of taking a tent down rather than setting it up or remaining inside it.

Araphōth, also rendered Arafoth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 17:19. The available lexical information identifies it as the name itself, but the verse text is not included here, so its specific role in that passage cannot be explained further without adding details not provided. Its meaning is therefore best stated as the personal or place name “Araphōth; Arafoth.”

This noun means “celebration of divine praises”—an expression for honoring God by proclaiming or celebrating his praiseworthy acts and qualities. It presents praise as a spoken or public acknowledgment of God’s greatness, rather than merely a private feeling. In the Greek LXX data, the word occurs once, in Sirach 36:13. Its precise emphasis in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and prayer context.

This verb means “best”: it describes being or performing best in comparison with others. As a verb, it expresses the action of being best rather than naming a person or quality. In the LXX material, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 2:18. The reference identifies its only occurrence, but without the verse text, the surrounding context cannot be explained further. Its central idea remains being best in relation to others.

Asabal, also rendered “Asaval,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 8:33. The available information identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain who bore it or what the immediate passage says about that person. Its meaning is therefore best stated as the personal name “Asabal” or “Asaval.”

This verb means to secure someone or something—to place it in a protected or firmly held condition. It describes an action of making something secure rather than merely noticing or possessing it. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times, appearing once in Isaiah and three times in Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being secured and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains firm protection or security.

Baithok, also rendered Vethok, is a proper name for a place rather than a word describing an action, quality, or teaching. It identifies a specific location in the Old Testament’s Greek translation. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 19:25. Because the available information does not include the verse’s wording or surrounding passage, the name’s precise role there cannot be explained further; its supported meaning is the place name itself.

This verb means “weighty; weigh down.” It describes making something heavy or burdened, whether literally or in a broader sense of pressing upon someone or something. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 45 times, so it is a recurring word for heaviness and burden. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what is being weighed down.

This word is a proper name, identified as “Bēsi” and “Visi.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general object; it functions as a name within the Greek Old Testament text. It occurs twice in the LXX corpus, both times in Nehemiah, at Nehemiah 7:52 and 10:19. Without the surrounding verse text, the available information does not establish whether it names a person, family, or place.

This Greek LXX adjective describes someone or something that is still young and dependent on milk—“sucking; young.” It points to an early stage of life, especially the condition of a nursing infant or other very young creature. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical Greek writings represented here, appearing once each in 1 Samuel, Amos, and Sirach. Its exact force in any one sentence depends on the noun it describes, but its central idea remains youth marked by nursing or immaturity.

This Greek LXX noun means “stylus” or “pencil,” a tool used for writing or marking. It names the instrument itself rather than an action, person, or idea. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Job 19:24. Its basic meaning remains that of a writing tool; the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This noun means “commander of ten,” referring to a person responsible for leading a group of ten. It describes an appointed position within an organized structure of leadership, alongside other commanders overseeing larger groups. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: three times in Exodus and Deuteronomy, and once in 1 Maccabees. The word therefore identifies a specific leadership role rather than merely describing the number ten.

gl: make to sit apart; set apart
d: make to sit apart; set apart

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “make to sit apart” or “set apart.” It describes causing someone or something to be placed separately rather than together with others. As a verb, it expresses an action of separating or assigning a distinct place. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Samuel 11:1. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being separated and why, but the word itself centers on making separate or setting apart.

This verb means “set on fire”: it describes putting something into a burning or flaming condition. It is an action word, focusing on the act of igniting or causing something to burn rather than naming the fire itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 3:15. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the exact object and force of the action must be understood from that passage’s context.

This verb means “let pass through.” It describes permitting movement through a place, boundary, or passage rather than stopping what is moving. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 3:13. That occurrence establishes its basic action, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what or whom it concerns there. It functions as an action word describing permission or passage.

Dōdam, also rendered Thotham, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 19:33, identifying a person or place named in that passage. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name’s specific role in Joshua 19:33 cannot be explained further. Its essential sense is simply the proper name “Dōdam” or “Thotham.”

Ezrikam is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears twice, both times in genealogical lists in 1 Chronicles. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide a separate definition or explain its meaning beyond its use as a proper name. Its significance in either passage therefore depends on the surrounding genealogy and the person being named.

This word means “descendant,” referring to someone who comes from a particular ancestor or family line. As an adjective, it describes people as belonging to a later generation or being descended from someone. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 33 times, showing a recurring way to identify family continuation across generations. Its precise reference—whether to children, grandchildren, or later offspring—depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains descent from an earlier ancestor.

This Greek LXX noun means “release”: the act of being set free, relieved, or let go. It names release as a thing or condition rather than describing an action by itself. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, appearing in Esther, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains release from a burden, restriction, or threatened condition.

This noun refers to an abortion or miscarriage—the loss or expulsion of a developing child before birth. It names the event itself rather than a person, action, or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Numbers, Job, and Ecclesiastes, where the surrounding passage determines its precise force. The word’s central meaning remains the same: a pregnancy ending before the expected birth, whether described as a miscarriage or an abortion.

This adverb means “openly” or “visibly,” describing something done in a way that can be plainly seen rather than hidden or concealed. It tells how an action or behavior appears to others. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Psalms, Proverbs, and Zephaniah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains clear: something is exposed to view or carried out in an unmistakable, public manner.

“Struggle bravely in” describes actively exerting oneself with courage within a difficult situation or task. It is a verb, so it presents this brave struggle as an action rather than merely naming a condition or quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 17:13. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is courageous effort under difficulty. It portrays determined engagement rather than passive endurance.

This verb means to report: to communicate or make information known. It describes the act of telling something so that others can hear or learn it. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs 12 times across Psalms, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its basic sense remains focused on reporting, while the surrounding sentence determines what information is being communicated and to whom. The word therefore points to an outward act of making something known rather than merely holding or understanding information privately.

“Run aground” is a verb describing a vessel reaching land or becoming stuck on the shore instead of continuing through the water. It expresses a physical stopping point caused by contact with land. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Proverbs 7:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the action of running aground.

This verb means “arouse”: to awaken, stir up, or cause someone or something to rise into action. It describes an act of bringing forth a response or movement rather than merely observing it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times, including passages from Samuel, Isaiah, Amos, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence says is being aroused.

This noun means “fairness,” describing the quality of dealing justly and treating others fairly. It identifies a quality rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, the word occurs nine times: twice in Old Testament passages and seven times in deuterocanonical books. Its precise emphasis can vary with the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains fairness and equitable treatment.

This Greek LXX verb means to consent—to agree to or approve something. It describes an act of willing agreement rather than merely hearing or considering a proposal. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this corpus, including Proverbs and Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what person or matter receives agreement, but its central idea remains giving approval or agreement.

This adjective means “ready” or “prepared”: in a state of readiness for an action, responsibility, journey, or appointed purpose. It can describe someone or something made suitable and available for what is required. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 56 times, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used broadly rather than for one narrow situation. The surrounding passage determines what the person or thing is ready for, but the word itself emphasizes readiness and preparedness.

This noun means “inquiry” or “inquest”: a deliberate effort to investigate, examine, or seek an answer. It refers to the act or process of questioning something rather than to a person who asks questions. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages from 1 Samuel, Ecclesiastes, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Hosea, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains careful investigation or examination.

“Ēmi; Imi” is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Ezra 2:57. Because no verse text or wider passage is provided here, the name itself does not establish the person’s role, family connection, or significance. Its normal function is simply personal identification, rather than describing an action, quality, object, or doctrine.

This verb means “brave”: it describes being courageous or acting without fear. In the Greek LXX, it functions as an action word, describing a person who is brave or urging someone to be brave. It occurs 18 times in the LXX corpus, spanning Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX noun means “hunter” or “huntsman”—a person who pursues and captures wild animals. It identifies someone by that activity rather than describing a spiritual quality or abstract idea. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, including passages in Psalms, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning remains a person engaged in hunting.

Iadai; Iathe is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily the individual’s name rather than a general concept. This LXX name occurs twice, in 1 Chronicles 2:47 and Ezra 10:43. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify which person is meant in each passage.

Ianōch, also rendered Ianokh, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 15:29. Because it is a personal or place name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it names someone or something in the biblical account. The available lexical information does not provide an additional ordinary definition or explain the name’s context beyond that single reference.

Iekonam is a proper name, functioning as a personal or place designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears one time, in Joshua 12:22. The available lexical information preserves the name as “Iekonam,” without supplying an additional common-language definition. Its exact reference in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage and verse text, not to the name’s basic lexical function.

Ieremeēl, also rendered Ieremil, is a proper personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies named individuals in genealogical and historical passages. This name occurs seven times across seven verses, appearing in 1 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Jeremiah. Its precise reference in any particular passage depends on the surrounding names and narrative context.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iesoua” or “Iesua,” used to identify a person rather than describe an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 46:17. Because it is a personal name, its basic meaning is the name itself; the surrounding verse is needed to identify the person and explain his role there.

“Iōaden; Ioathen” is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is preserved as a personal designation rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text, at 2 Chronicles 25:1. The available wording does not provide an additional descriptive meaning for the name, and the verse text is not available here to explain its particular contextual role.

This adjective describes something that is at the right place—properly situated or fitting where it belongs. It points to suitability of position rather than merely being present. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 15:23. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what is being described there, but the word itself presents the idea of being appropriately placed. Its central sense is therefore “at the right place.”

This Greek LXX verb means “inscribe”: to write or mark words onto a surface so they are recorded. It describes the act of putting something into written form, rather than merely speaking or remembering it. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages from Exodus, Chronicles, Job, Hosea, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being written and the surrounding context.

This LXX word describes something positioned opposite another thing or located before it. It can function as an adverb or preposition, marking a place, position, or direction in relation to someone or something else. Its central idea is being face-to-face with, in front of, or situated before another. The word occurs 73 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, with “before” as its more frequent English rendering and “opposite” also appearing.

This word means “secretly”: it describes an action done out of sight or without being openly known. As an adverb, it tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 13:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains concealed or private action.

This Greek LXX noun means “surrounding”: the state or action of being around something. It points to an encircling arrangement or movement rather than to the thing located in the center. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Numbers, Psalms, and Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being surrounded and on the surrounding sentence.

Labōs, also rendered Lavos, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:32. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s specific referent must be determined from that passage. Its basic meaning is therefore its identity as the proper name “Labōs” or “Lavos,” not a broader concept or theological term.

This noun refers to a “stone of Liguria,” identifying a particular precious or ornamental stone associated with that region. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Exodus and once in Ezekiel. The word appears in descriptions involving lists or settings of valuable stones, but the available text does not provide enough context to define its color, appearance, or symbolic significance more precisely. Its basic meaning is therefore the name of a Ligurian stone.

This adjective means “painful”—something that causes or involves pain, distress, or sorrow. It describes a painful condition, experience, or matter rather than naming a person or object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom writings, it occurs six times, including four occurrences in Proverbs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the noun or situation it describes, but the central idea remains that of pain or distress.

This noun means “scourge,” referring to an instrument or means of severe punishment and suffering. It can describe a physical whip, or more broadly a painful affliction or destructive blow. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, the word occurs 33 times, including passages from Kings, Psalms, Job, and the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence: it may point to punishment inflicted by people or to suffering experienced as a scourge. The central idea remains something harsh that strikes, chastens, or causes distress.

This noun means “cloud,” referring to a visible mass in the sky. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs 131 times, showing that it is a normal word for a cloud rather than a rare expression. It appears in passages ranging from Genesis through Deuteronomy and later writings. The surrounding context determines whether a particular cloud is being described simply as part of the created world or in connection with a scene involving God’s presence.

This word means “illegitimate,” describing someone or something regarded as lacking a lawful or recognized standing. It functions as an adjective, so it identifies a person or thing by that condition rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 4:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic meaning remains a description of illegitimacy or nonrecognized status.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Obdia” or “Ovthia.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:3. Since the available record provides the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific role in that genealogy cannot be explained further here. The word’s basic function is simply to identify a person.

This noun means “ruin” or “destruction,” referring to the condition or outcome in which something is brought to ruin. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs 22 times, so it is a recurring word rather than a rare expression. It appears across both the Old Testament books and the deuterocanonical writings included in this corpus. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Ornan is a proper name—the personal name of a man. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 21:21. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its basic meaning is simply the identification of Ornan as an individual. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what Ornan does or why he matters in that verse; the name itself does not express an action, quality, or spiritual idea.

This noun means “mastery over passion”: the ability to govern powerful feelings or desires rather than be ruled by them. It describes inner self-control and purposeful command over emotional impulses. In its Greek LXX usage, the word appears twice, both in 4 Maccabees, so its ordinary sense is clear even though the supplied material does not include the surrounding verse text. The word points to disciplined control of passion, not the removal of all feeling. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: knife worn beside the sword; dirk
d: knife worn beside the sword; dirk

e.t: This noun means “knife worn beside the sword; dirk,” referring to a smaller blade carried alongside a sword. It describes a weapon rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 5:8. The precise role of the knife in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies a companion knife intended for carrying beside a sword.

This Greek LXX preposition means “besides,” pointing to something considered in addition to another person or thing. It helps mark an added item or distinguish what stands apart from what has already been mentioned. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament books and once in the deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central function is to indicate what is besides or beyond the item under discussion.

This word means “coat,” referring to an outer garment worn over the body. It is a noun describing clothing rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears five times, including passages in Genesis, Daniel, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a coat or outer covering.

This Greek LXX verb means to mislead someone or to wander from the right path. It can describe a person who strays physically, but it can also express being led astray or moving away from what is true and right. The word appears 116 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is used across a broad range of passages rather than for one unusual situation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes leading another astray or wandering oneself.

This Greek LXX verb means “fulfill” or “fill.” It describes bringing something to fullness, making it complete, or filling a space or measure. Depending on the sentence, it can refer either to something being physically filled or to an appointed matter reaching completion. The word occurs 95 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, so it is used across a broad range of settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being filled or fulfilled.

This verb means to act maliciously or to intend harm. It describes a person whose purpose or conduct is wicked toward others, rather than merely someone who experiences difficulty or misfortune. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 27 times, so it expresses a recurring description of harmful intent or behavior. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains purposeful wrongdoing directed against someone else.

This noun refers to a guard positioned in front—someone or something placed ahead to protect, watch, or secure a place. Its central idea is a forward guard or protective post, rather than guarding in a general or undefined sense. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 12 times, appearing especially in passages connected with watchfulness and defense. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to the guard itself or the protective position it occupies.

This adjective means “fiery red,” describing a vivid red color. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for things or appearances marked by this striking redness, including objects and visionary sights. The word occurs eight times in seven Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Song of Songs, with several occurrences in Zechariah. Its basic sense remains focused on color rather than describing a person’s character, an action, or a spiritual quality.

Raphain is a proper name, rendered also as Rhafen, rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a named person or group in the Greek Old Testament and is preserved as a name in English translations. This LXX word occurs seven times across six verses, from Genesis through Joshua, with most occurrences in Deuteronomy. Its exact reference in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains that of a proper name.

This adjective describes something patched or stitched together. It refers to material joined by sewing, rather than a single unjoined piece. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears twice, both times in Exodus, at Exodus 27:16 and Exodus 37:21. Its central idea is a fabric or material made ready through stitching or patching. The exact object being described depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself points to something sewn together.

gl: inclination downwards; sinking of the scale
d: inclination downwards; sinking of the scale

e.t: This noun describes an inclination downward, especially the sinking or lowering of a scale. It names a downward movement or a shift toward one side rather than an upward rise or balanced position. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs seven times, including passages from Joshua, Proverbs, Isaiah, Wisdom, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a downward turn, settling, or weighing movement.

This adjective describes someone as “strong of body,” emphasizing physical strength or robust bodily condition. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Maccabees 12:27. As an adjective, it describes a person rather than naming an action or object. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning points to bodily strength and physical capability.

This word is the proper name Samaria, referring to a place named in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. It is not a description or action but a geographic name used to identify Samaria in biblical history. The word occurs 114 times in the Greek LXX corpus, beginning in 1 Kings and continuing through 2 Maccabees. Most occurrences appear in 1–2 Kings, showing its frequent use in accounts involving the northern kingdom and its surrounding history.

This verb means “eat flesh.” It describes the act of consuming flesh as food, rather than naming a person, object, or general condition. As a verb, it expresses an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:26. The word itself simply denotes eating flesh in plain, direct terms; the surrounding passage determines why that action is mentioned there.

This word is a proper personal name, rendered “Sarouias” or “Saroias.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 21 times, especially in 2 Samuel, and also appears in 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, and Jeremiah. Its exact reference in any passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative, since the name itself simply identifies the person being mentioned.

This word means “shekel” or “coin,” a noun naming a unit of money. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used when amounts of money are stated, so it identifies what is being counted or given rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 75 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, and the historical books.
